question_text:
The circuit below uses a resistor voltage divider to produce a reference voltage for an ADC. A black box sits between the divider output and the ADC input.

What belongs in the black box, and why is it necessary?
answer_text:
A voltage follower — an op-amp wired with its output fed directly back to its inverting (−) input.

▶ Detailed Explanation

The voltage divider has a source impedance of R₁ ∥ R₂. If the ADC draws current from that node it forms a second voltage divider with the source impedance, shifting the measured voltage. The voltage follower fixes this by presenting near-infinite input impedance to the divider. Real op-amps have input impedances in the MΩ–GΩ range, so their input current is only nanoamps to picoamps — effectively zero. The output current the ADC needs is supplied by the op-amp's power rails (V+ / V−), not by R₁ or R₂.

Loading Effect Without a Buffer

With R₁ = R₂ = 10 kΩ and Vcc = 5 V, open-circuit Vmid = 2.5 V. With a 10 kΩ ADC input impedance in parallel with R₂:

  • R_effective = 10k ∥ 10k = 5 kΩ
  • V_measured = 5 V × 5k / (10k + 5k) = 1.67 V
  • Error: 0.83 V — a 33% measurement error

With the Voltage Follower

The op-amp input draws ≈ 0 A, so R_ADC in parallel with R₂ has no effect on Vmid. The divider sees no load and the ADC reads exactly 2.5 V.
bonus_question_text: When can you get away without a voltage follower?
bonus_answer_text:
Two situations:

  1. The datasheet covers you. Every ADC datasheet specifies a maximum allowable source impedance (often in the acquisition time section, sometimes labeled "R_source max"). If R₁ ∥ R₂ is comfortably below that value, no external buffer is needed.
  2. Slow sampling + decoupling capacitor. Place a capacitor (e.g. 100 nF) directly at the ADC input pin. Between samples it pre-charges to the correct voltage through the divider, then supplies the burst of charge when the ADC's acquisition switch closes. Only works if your sample rate is low enough that the RC settling time (τ = R₁∥R₂ × C) fits within the gap between conversions.
